questions.text: If you type java MyClass after compiling with javac MyClass.java, what exactly happens?
options: JVM directly executes .java file line by line
JVM loads .class file, verifies bytecode, and executes using JIT/Interpreter
The java command recompiles .java file to .class before execution
The command simply prints bytecode stored inside .class file

questions.text: Bytecode in Java is created at which stage?
options: At runtime, by JVM after interpreting the .java file
During compilation of .java file into .class file by javac
When .class file is loaded into memory by JVM

questions.text: The compiled Java bytecode stored in .class file is actually:
Which of the following is a wrong feature attributed to Java?
options: Java is platform independent due to JVM
Java is 100% Object-Oriented (even primitive data types are objects)
Java provides automatic memory management via Garbage Collector
Java supports multithreading as a built-in feature

questions.text: In the expression int x = (5 > 10) ? 20 : 30;, what happens internally?
options: JVM evaluates both 20 and 30 before choosing
Only the selected expression (30) is evaluated
Compiler replaces ternary with if-else during compilation
It throws compile-time error since ternary doesn’t support integers

questions.text: Java is called platform independent because:
options: Bytecode can run on any OS without JVM
JVM converts bytecode into native machine code for that OS
Source code is directly understood by all platforms
Compiled bytecode is same as machine-level assembly

questions.text: What happens if a local variable inside a method has the same name as an instance variable?
options: Local variable shadows the instance variable within that method

questions.text: Which keyword cannot be used with a local variable?

options: Platform dependent because it’s written separately for each OS
Written in Java, so it’s portable everywhere

questions.text: Which of the following is TRUE about Java’s history?
options: Java was initially named “Oak,” developed at Sun Microsystems by James Gosling in 1991
It was first intended for digital consumer devices like set-top boxes
The first public version (Java 1.0) was released in 1995
